title: Spelling & One-Word Substitution
intro: Two quick-scoring areas sit together here. Spelling questions ask you to pick the correctly (or incorrectly) spelt word — a few rules plus a list of habitual offenders cover most of them. One-word substitution asks for the single word that replaces a phrase ('a person who eats everything' → omnivore); these come from a finite, repeatable pool. Both reward recognition, so steady exposure is the whole game.

items.name: Double the consonant
items.formula: before -ed/-ing on short-vowel words: stop → stopping

items.name: One-word sub method
items.formula: identify the key idea, then recall the term

topics.name: Spelling Rules
topics.details: A few rules cover most spelling items: 'I before E except after C'; double the final consonant when adding -ed/-ing to a stressed short-vowel syllable; drop a silent 'e' before a vowel suffix but keep it before a consonant suffix.

topics.name: Commonly Misspelt Words
topics.details: A short list of words causes most spelling errors. Learn the exact letter pattern of each — SSC usually offers three wrong spellings and one right one.

solved.solution: Separate ("there is A RAT in separate").

topics.name: One-Word Substitution (People)
topics.details: Many one-word-substitution items name a kind of person. Identify the key trait in the phrase, then recall the term. The pool is finite and repeats.

solved.problem: One who studies the stars and planets.
A person who cannot read or write.
A person who is 100 years old or more.

unsolved.problem: One who does not believe in God.

topics.name: One-Word Substitution (General)
topics.details: Other one-word substitutions describe situations or things. The prefixes (in-, im-, un-) and roots usually point straight to the answer.

solved.problem: A speech made without prior preparation.
An animal living both on land and in water.

unsolved.problem: A place where money is coined.

shortcuts: Learn the spelling rules (i before e; double the consonant; drop/keep silent e).
Memorise the habitual offenders (accommodation, occurrence, separate, definitely).
For one-word substitution, isolate the key idea, then recall the term.
Prefixes/roots point to the answer (in-/im- = not, somn- = sleep, biblio- = books).
Both areas are recognition — steady exposure beats last-minute cramming.
mistakes: Single vs double letters (accommodation, embarrass, committee).
"seperate" and "definately" — both wrong; it is separate, definitely.
Picking a related but inexact one-word substitute.
Forgetting "i before e except after c".
pyq: SSC asks one "pick the correctly spelt word" item and one or two one-word substitutions per Tier 1, drawn from a repeatable pool. Recognition built through practice is the whole skill.
summary: Spelling is rules plus a list of habitual offenders; one-word substitution is a finite, learnable pool. Apply "i before e", consonant-doubling and silent-e rules, memorise the tricky spellings, and decode substitutions from their key idea and prefixes. Both are pure recognition marks.
